text: 'We rolled out Conditional Access to 100% of users' is a real fact, and it is not proof that zero trust is working. It's proof a project finished. Coverage can hit 100% while an attacker's path to lateral movement stays essentially unchanged, if the deployed policies were loose or privileged accounts got a temporary exemption nobody ever revisited.

That's the split this lesson draws. Implementation metrics answer 'did we build it' -- percent of endpoints enrolled, number of segmentation policies written, whether MFA is enabled. They're real, but a skeptical CISO has learned to distrust them, because they can stay true while risk stays flat. Outcome metrics answer the harder question: did real risk actually go down?

Start with standing privileged access -- count how many accounts hold always-on admin rights right now, and watch that number fall as PAM and just-in-time elevation take hold: two hundred standing domain admins down to three, the rest requesting access for thirty minutes when they need it. Then there's mean time to detect lateral movement -- run a controlled test and measure how long monitoring takes to flag movement between hosts or identities. Before segmentation, that's often days. After it, minutes, because the movement now crosses a boundary that generates a signal.

A third: what percent of traffic actually passes through an explicit, identity- and device-aware policy decision, versus being allowed just because it originated inside a trusted zone? Moving that from fifteen percent to eighty-five percent is a direct measure of how much of the old 'trust the network' model is actually gone. And report MFA coverage by population, not blended -- a headline ninety-two percent can hide that every admin account is still on a phishable factor.

Two more worth tracking: mean time to revoke access after a role or employment change, which catches the classic failure where access was correct on day one and silently wrong a year later; and segmentation violations actually caught, where a rising count right after rollout is often a good sign -- it means the segmentation is doing real work, not that something broke.

Put the strongest of these into a plain before-and-after table: standing admins, detection time, verified traffic percent, each with the mechanism that changed it. No acronyms doing the explaining, no single composite score carrying the whole story. Next lesson takes that same table and turns it into language an executive who has never heard of Conditional Access will actually trust.
